title: The book of life
hookLine: Nand Lal's Zindagi Nama speaks of the longing to see the Beloved in everything

lines: A NAME ON A SHOP SIGN.
cards: Someone who's just fallen in love sees the beloved's name on a shop sign. Hears their laugh in a stranger's voice across a train platform. Smells their coat in a crowded elevator.
The world hasn't changed. The one looking at it has. Bhai Nand Lal took that ordinary, slightly ridiculous experience, made it into a whole way of seeing, and pointed it at God.
He gave the book a plain title. Today: Zindagi Nama.

teach.h: ZINDAGI NAMA: THE BOOK OF LIFE.
teach.b: Zindagi means life. Nama, a book or a letter. The book of life.
It's a poem, written in Persian, in the language of love poetry. Here is its center.
Nand Lal writes of a longing to see the Beloved, meaning God, and of the strange thing that happens when that longing takes hold: the Beloved begins to show up everywhere, wherever the eye falls.
For the one who longs, there's nowhere the Beloved isn't. Turn that over a few ways. First, the longing isn't a problem to be cured.
In the Zindagi Nama, wanting to see is itself part of the path. The ache is a kind of attention. Second, the seeing is the reward.
Not a vision in a far-off place, not a reward after death.

teach.h: A WAY OF LOOKING, FOR A LIFE.
teach.b: A changed way of looking, here, at ordinary things. Third, it fits the Guru's word Nand Lal knew. Sikhs hear the Guru Granth Sahib speak of the One pervading everything, in every heart, in water and land.
Nand Lal says it in the language of a lover who can't stop seeing the beloved's face.
And fourth, it's for a life, not a moment. The title says so: a book of life, a way to walk through all of it with your eyes open. Nand Lal doesn't promise the longing ever goes quiet.
He seems to treat it as a good companion for the whole road.

how: Sikhs read Bhai Nand Lal's Zindagi Nama in Persian and in translation, and its verses are recited and sung as poems of longing for the Divine.

o: a Persian list of Sikh rules for daily life
Nand Lal's Persian book of life and longing
a diary of the Guru's court, day by day

games.q: inside the book — tap the pairs.

s: the Zindagi Nama is written in Persian
Nand Lal wrote it in Persian, a great language of love poetry.
the Beloved in the Zindagi Nama is a human lover
the Beloved is God; Nand Lal uses a lover's language to speak of the Divine.
Nand Lal says the Beloved is seen in one holy place only
the poem speaks of the longing to see the Beloved in everything.

games.q: you long to see God, and the longing won't go away. what does the Zindagi Nama do with it?
o: treat it as a problem to cure.
make it part of the path, until the Beloved shows up everywhere.
save it for a vision after death.
games.why: in the book of life, the longing is part of the path, and its reward is a changed way of seeing: the Beloved in everything.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing within reach, a cup, a plant on the sill, the light on a wall, your own hand, and look at it the way a lover looks: slowly, as if it might be about to say something.
When your eyes want to move on, stay one breath longer, and if you pray, you can say Waheguru to what you see.

wordCard.voice: Zindagi Nama, Nand Lal's Persian poem of longing to see the Beloved, until the Beloved is seen in everything.

carryVoice: Your line: see him everywhere. The world stays the same; the looking changes. Day seven hundred fourteen, done.

sources.ref: Bhai Nand Lal Goya, Zindagi Nama (longing to see the Beloved; the Beloved in all things)
